extractions.quote: The stiff-man syndrome is reported in a 55-year-old woman who also had signs of severe bulbar musculature hypercontraction. These clinical features correspond to the progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity syndrome. Diazepam was minimally beneficial, but after treatment with plasmapheresis and corticosteroids, she was still asymptomatic when seen 5 years later. CSF fluid was normal, including IgG synthesis and myelin basic protein, and no oligoclonal bands were present. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the head without contrast were normal. Serum antibodies against GABAergic synapses were not detected in pre- and postplasmapheresis sera.

extractions.quote: Diazepam, 15 mg orally four times daily, markedly diminished extensor spasms. EMG repeated 3 weeks later while the patient was receiving diazepam, 15 mg three times daily, showed substantial improvement. In late August, nausea and vomiting precluded taking diazepam, and the patient was readmitted because of severe trunk rigidity, urinary retention, near total ophthalmoplegia, trismus, and inability to swallow. Intravenous administration of 5 mg diazepam had no effect, and pulmonary arrest necessitated ventilator-dependent intubation, later requiring tracheotomy. Dantrolene sodium, carbamazepine, carbidopa-levodopa, and phenytoin were ineffective. Medications included diazepam, 20 mg daily; azathioprine, 50 mg daily; and prednisone, 15 mg daily. In 1994, the patient still had no hypercontraction symptoms, signs, or diplopia. Medications included prednisone, 5 mg daily; azathioprine, 50 mg daily; and no diazepam.
